desc:
Each building is described by buildings[i] = [left, right, height]: it occupies the x-range from left to right (so its width is right - left) and rises from the ground (y = 0) to height. Buildings may overlap or touch. The skyline is the region under the highest building at every x; places covered by no building have height 0.

Return the area of the largest axis-aligned rectangle that fits entirely inside this skyline region.

Example: [[0,4,2],[2,6,3],[5,9,1]]. The skyline has height 2 on [0,2], 3 on [2,6] (the second building covers the first there), and 3 until x=6, then 1 on [6,9]. The best rectangle is x in [2,6] with height 3... or x in [0,9] with height 1, area 9; the largest is 12 (x from 0 to 6 at height 2).
constraints: The answer fits in a signed 32-bit integer (it is at most 10<sup>9</sup>)
hints: First turn the overlapping buildings into a skyline: a list of consecutive x-segments, each with a single height. Coordinates are large, so work with the building edges only.

Sweep the sorted x-coordinates of all edges. For each segment between two neighbouring edges, the height is the maximum height among the buildings that cover it (a max-heap with lazy removal of buildings that have ended works well).

Now it is the classic largest rectangle in a histogram, except that bars have different widths: keep a stack of (start x, height); when a lower segment arrives, pop and compute height * (x - start), then push the lower segment with the popped start.
editorial: Any rectangle inside the skyline can be slid down to the ground, so we only need rectangles that sit on y = 0. Their area is limited by the lowest part of the skyline over their x-range, which is a largest-rectangle-in-a-histogram problem, with bars of variable width because the skyline has long flat stretches.

Step 1: collect all distinct edge coordinates and sort them. Sweep them left to right; push the buildings whose left edge is at or before the current x into a max-heap keyed by height; discard from the top of the heap buildings whose right edge is not beyond the current x; the height of the segment starting here is the top of the heap or 0. Step 2: run the histogram stack on the segments, storing (start x, height); when a segment of height h arrives, pop every entry with height ≥ h, record height * (x - start), and push h at the smallest start that was popped. A final sentinel of height 0 flushes the stack. With E = 2n edges, the sweep costs O(n log n) and the stack pass O(n).
solution:
import heapq


def largestSkylineRectangle(buildings):
    xs = sorted({x for l, r, h in buildings for x in (l, r)})
    order = sorted(buildings)
    heap = []
    j = 0
    segments = []
    for k in range(len(xs) - 1):
        x = xs[k]
        while j < len(order) and order[j][0] <= x:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (-order[j][2], order[j][1]))
            j += 1
        while heap and heap[0][1] <= x:
            heapq.heappop(heap)
        height = -heap[0][0] if heap else 0
        segments.append((x, height))
    segments.append((xs[-1], 0))   # sentinel: ground level after the last edge
    stack = []   # (start x, height) with increasing heights
    best = 0
    for x, height in segments:
        start = x
        while stack and stack[-1][1] >= height:
            s, h = stack.pop()
            best = max(best, h * (x - s))
            start = s
        stack.append((start, height))
    return best
